segments.say: It's one of the oldest questions in the world. Can money buy happiness? Some people say, of course not, the best things in life are free. Others say, anyone who says money can't buy happiness has never been poor. Both sides have a point. And in recent years, researchers have studied this question with remarkable amounts of data.

In two thousand and ten, two Nobel prize winners, the psychologist Daniel Kahneman and the economist Angus Deaton, published an influential study. They analyzed survey answers from about four hundred and fifty thousand people in the United States. And they distinguished between two kinds of happiness.

show.what: An analysis of survey answers from about 450,000 Americans, looking at how income relates to everyday emotional well-being and to overall life evaluation.

segments.say: The first kind is how you feel day to day. Your everyday emotions. Are you often joyful, stressed, sad, relaxed? The second kind is how you evaluate your life overall, when you step back and think about it. How satisfied are you with your life as a whole? These two can be quite different.

Kahneman and Deaton found that life evaluation kept rising with income. But for everyday emotional well being, they reported that the benefits seemed to level off above a certain income, around seventy five thousand dollars a year in the United States at that time. Above that, more money didn't seem to make the average day feel much better.

That number, seventy five thousand, became famous. It was quoted in articles, books and conversations around the world, often in a simplified way. Money makes you happier, up to a point, and then it stops. It was a neat story. But science has a habit of revisiting neat stories.

In two thousand and twenty one, the researcher Matthew Killingsworth published a study with a different method. Instead of asking people how they felt yesterday, he used a smartphone app that asked people at random moments how they were feeling right now. More than thirty three thousand people, and more than one point seven million moments.

show.where: University of Pennsylvania, published in PNAS, 2021
show.what: Over 1.7 million experience-sampling reports from more than 33,000 employed US adults, collected through a smartphone app, linking income to how people felt in the moment.

segments.say: And Killingsworth found no plateau. In his data, everyday well being kept rising with income, well beyond seventy five thousand dollars. The two findings seemed to contradict each other. So something unusual happened. The researchers decided to work together to resolve the disagreement.

This is called an adversarial collaboration. Researchers who disagree team up, with a neutral partner, to find the truth together. In two thousand and twenty three, Killingsworth and Kahneman, with Barbara Mellers as a mediator, published their joint findings. And the answer turned out to be more interesting than either original story.

show.what: An "adversarial collaboration": researchers with opposing findings re-analyzed the data together, with the help of a mediator, Barbara Mellers.

segments.say: They found that, for most people, happiness continued to rise with income, even at higher levels. But for the least happy group, roughly the unhappiest fifth of people, happiness rose with income up to around one hundred thousand dollars a year, and then leveled off. For them, beyond a certain point, money couldn't fix what was making them unhappy.

show.cap: It depends on how happy you are.

segments.say: That makes intuitive sense. Money is very good at solving certain problems. Paying bills, reducing stress, getting healthcare, having a safety net. But some sources of unhappiness, like loneliness, grief, or illness, can't be solved by money. Once the money problems are solved, those other problems remain.

It's also worth knowing that, in these studies, the effect of income on happiness is real, but not enormous. Many other things, like relationships, health, purpose and how we spend our time, matter a great deal too. Money is one ingredient in a good life. An important one, especially when it's scarce. But not the only one.

show.cap: The effect is real, but modest.

segments.say: And perhaps most importantly, research suggests that how you spend money may matter as much as how much you have. Two people with the same income can get very different amounts of happiness from it, depending on what they do with it. And that's what we'll explore next.

So can money buy happiness? A fair answer might be this. Money can buy a lot of the conditions for happiness. Safety, comfort, freedom, time. It tends to help more when you have less. And it works best when it's spent on the things that truly matter to you.

show.cap: Money is one ingredient, not the whole recipe

segments.say: So here's what the research suggests. Life satisfaction tends to rise with income. For most people, everyday well being keeps rising too. For the least happy, the gains level off beyond a certain point. And how we spend our money matters a great deal.

show.title: Money and happiness

For most people, everyday mood keeps rising too
For the unhappiest, gains level off
How you spend matters a lot

segments.say: So what kinds of spending seem to bring the most happiness? Researchers have tested a few surprising ideas. Spending on other people. Buying experiences. And even buying something we rarely think of as for sale. Time. Let's explore them next.
